anchor: Casey Reas, Chandler McWilliams and LUST, Form+Code in Design, Art, and Architecture (Princeton Architectural Press, 2010 [mem]; 176 pp. [V]). Its themes Repeat, Transform, Parameterize, Visualize, Simulate, each with two code examples (Embedded Iteration, Recursive Tree; Transcoded Landscape, Slit-Scan; Chair, Wave; Displaying Data, Superformula; Particles, Diffusion-Limited Aggregation) [V formandcode.com, fetched 2026-10-01], opened by 'What is Code?' and 'Form and Computers' [mem]. Applied to 3D bodies in Godot 4.6.
title: Form+Code for Bodies: repeat, transform, parameterize, visualize, simulate
thesis: This course is ordered by what code does to form, not by the order of Ada's halls. First you learn what code is and make single bodies: a point, a line, a room you can stand in with the headset on. Then you REPEAT a body (a trace, a grid, a tile, disorder in the grid, a tree that repeats inside itself), TRANSFORM it (a pivot, a scale, an easing, time laid into space, a function turned into ground), PARAMETERIZE it (a class, a family in the Inspector, a budget you measure, genes saved as files), VISUALIZE what cannot be seen (a value as colour, a noise field, a shader, an implicit surface, a graph, a judgment), and finally SIMULATE it (forces, aggregation, balance, rules, soft bodies, swarms, navigation, learning) until the model meets what it cannot hold. Each verb needs the ones before it: disorder is invisible without a grid, a transform means most when there are many bodies, an argument about a family needs a class, and a simulation needs all of these. The Ada halls carry each step or are visited as field trips. Where this order leaves the spine's order the chapter says why, and where a topic comes back (chance, colour, recursion, graphs) it is a named return. In every chapter you build a body in code, vary it along one axis, write down before rendering which two variants will look most alike, and defend one sentence with the picture. Then you ask what the approximation owes or hides, and you take the body out of the lab into a place where a body meets it.

parts.title: Code and Form (What is code? Form and computers)
parts.promise: You can make a single body in code, give it a collider that is a separate decision, place it by coordinates, relate two bodies with a function, bring in a scanned body, and stand among them in the headset from a build you exported.

parts.title: Repeat
parts.promise: You can make many bodies from one: a kept walk, a lattice, an authored surface, a tiled floor, a seeded disorder and a recursive tree, and you know that each repetition is decided by a gap, a rule, a seed or a stop.

parts.title: Transform
parts.promise: You can turn a body (pivots, scale, easing) and transcode one thing into another (time into space, a function into ground), and you have opened the player body itself as one transform among others.

parts.title: Parameterize (an addition to the spine, declared)
parts.promise: You can write a body as a class whose exported fields make a family, sweep one axis into a comparison sheet, measure what each value costs, test a claim, and save a body as a file that returns.

parts.title: Visualize
parts.promise: You can make an invisible value visible (colour, a noise field, a per-pixel shader, an implicit surface, a graph, a classifier) and say what each picture hides.

parts.title: Simulate
parts.promise: You can let bodies be made by processes (forces, aggregation, balance, rules, soft deformation, collectives, navigation, learning), assemble a small complete game, and end with a hall that argues and knows the limits of its own model.

chapters.title: Point Zero: the engine calls you
chapters.body: Two columns at the hall's entrance. One grows by a fixed amount every frame, the other by delta (seconds). The kit's greeting is set once in _ready(); the counts change in _process().

argument.axis: frame rate the scene runs at (--fixed-fps)
argument.predict: After five seconds the four delta-grown columns will be identical, so any two of them are the closest pair. The frame-grown columns will differ in proportion, and 90 and 120 will look most alike of those.
argument.claim: Only a body grown by delta is the same body on every machine: a headset at 90 Hz and a laptop at 60 Hz grow two different frame-bodies.

chapters.debt: A frame is not a second, and the device decides how many there are, so the headset's refresh rate becomes part of the body. Headless runs draw no frames at all (a documented Ada trap), so a rule that counts frames behaves differently there.

chapters.title: Point Lines: a relation between two bodies
chapters.body: A line between two carried points, drawn with the supplied SKETCH helper line(a, b); the student writes thickness_for(a, b) that returns a thickness from b - a and its length, so three lines of 0.5, 1 and 2 m carry an argument.

argument.axis: exponent p in thickness = 0.05 * length^p (three lines of 0.5, 1 and 2 m in each variant)
argument.predict: p = -1 and p = 1 will use about the same total ink and so look closest in weight, but read in opposite directions; p = 2 is the outlier, with its long line five times thicker than at p = 0.
argument.claim: A line's thickness is an argument about distance: one exponent turns the same three relations into strain or attraction.

chapters.debt: A line does not exist in 3D. Godot has no line(): it is a stretched box, or a one-pixel strip the headset draws with no thickness. chapters.body: A fan body, the triangles repeated around a centre: make_fan(n, radius, height) returns an ArrayMesh built with SurfaceTool, and a ConvexPolygonShape3D is made from the same points.

argument.claim: Light reads a surface through its normals, not its vertices: the same eight triangles become a crystal, a cone or a hole.

chapters.debt: Godot winds front faces clockwise, and when the winding is wrong the body is invisible from outside: a hole. Smooth shading lies about polycount, since the 'smooth' cone is 8 facets pretending, which is the first form of the application's polycount question. The convex hull fills in the open corner, so the collider lies too.

argument.claim: The same rotation makes a different body depending on where the pivot sits: a joint is a decision about where a body may bend.

chapters.debt: Euler angles lie: rotation order matters (Y then X is not X then Y) and gimbal lock is real. The Basis is the truth; the three numbers in the Inspector are an approximation of it. A skeleton imposes an anatomy, so queer the joint: put one where no anatomy has it.

chapters.title: Particles and aggregation: many short lives build one body
chapters.body: Diffusion-limited aggregation: random walkers are released, wander, and freeze when they touch the growing cluster; the frozen walkers are skinned into one mesh. Beside it, a GPUParticles3D emitter shows what short lives look like when nothing is kept.

learned_from: Form+Code (the anchor) [V themes and code examples]: name the parts by what code does to form, not by language feature. Repeat before Transform (the opposite of spine 2-3); recursion filed under Repeat; Parameterize as its own verb, which Ada's spine lacks although 74% of its scripts are built that way. Each theme has an essay and a precedent gallery, the model for each chapter's lineage and for the final.md. The anchor has no exercises, no skill ladder and no critique, so the course had to add all three.

Processing Handbook, 1st ed. [V]: a Synthesis checkpoint closes each part (ch6, ch12, ch17, ch21, ch37), and there are two tables of contents: the course's reading order and a by-spine index (in the markdown), so a departure shows as a jump in spine numbers. Static before continuous is kept only partly, because Godot calls your code from Point Zero on.

10 PRINT [V contents]: Regularity comes before Randomness, so chance sits straight after the grid and the tile (ch11), not at spine place 10. 'Ports' become declared returns (the tile ported to a shader at ch24), and 'Maze Walker' becomes a place (ch34).

Code as Creative Medium [V/agg]: Unpredictability after iteration and conditionals; named body prompts for the short-track mini project (Virtual Creature, Parametric Object, Extrapolated Body, Personal Prosthetic); short exercises (CODE) kept apart from open assignments (BODY plus ARGUMENT); 'Computing without a Computer' as Day Zero.

Aesthetic Programming [V]: a critical theme tied to each piece of syntax with no separate theory track, which is how DEBT sits inside each chapter; pause weeks in the long track; the final project planned two units before the end (ch35); the ReadMe beside the code in Git (ch37).

Critical Code Studies (Marino) and CCSWG [V]: the lookup table as a code-critique station modelled on Kittler's raytracer (ch25); a confessing debt comment in the student's own code (Climategate [mem]); 'describe a body in a single class' (ch18); write first, then read the debt; the forum-style critique thread (ch37).
Montfort, Exploratory Programming [V]: errors on day one ('valid and intentional are different', ch1); 'Critique My Starter Programs' turned on Godot's own capsule player (ch14).

Recreating the Past (SFPC) [V]: recreate a precedent (Nees's Schotter, Molnar, 10 PRINT, Durer's Melencolia) as the baseline for the ARGUMENT, with the difference as the DEBT; its close in Body and then Glitch/Deformation mirrors this course's close in soft bodies and critical simulation.
Code Societies (SFPC, 3 weeks) [V]: the short track's length and guest-session rhythm; 'Critical Simulation' as the model for ch36, the Ada addition Form+Code lacks.

Klee, Pedagogical Sketchbook [V via the braid's OCR read]: pendulum, circle, spiral is one derivation (ch16, under Transform); balance and falling (ch30); Part I's bone, tendon and muscle (ch13); the book ends in colour, which supports colour late as a system (ch22).
Albers, Interaction of Color [V]: fix the material and vary one thing (the family); 'one colour appears as two' as ch22's argument.
Gaboury, Image Objects [V contents]: the default body (ch3, ch14), the frame buffer (ch24) and object orientation (ch18) as chapter-grain debt readings.

The Nature of Code [V]: a cumulative chapter-end project that is literally a museum exhibit of creatures, which is why project_step always adds to the student's hall; the NoC order is kept inside Simulate (forces, particles, physics libraries, CA, fractals-as-rules, agents, evolution, networks).

GDQuest [V]: use before make (the SKETCH helper, the walker, the pickup are used first and opened later) and the skin/controller split (ch13), which is what lets the desktop body be swapped for the XR body.
Chun, Programmed Visions [V contents]: 'sourcery' is named at the first supplied helper that gets opened (ch5) and again at ch36, so the course does not claim that reading code reveals everything.

What no comparable course had and Ada supplies: a written, falsifiable prediction of the closest pair before every render (after dna.predicted_degeneracy), and the BODY and PLACE strands in 3D and VR. All the canon courses are 2D and web-first.
